title: Book of Changes (Yijing)
creator: Authors of the Book of Changes
location: Zhou China; received text fixed in the Han
description: The Yijing, or Zhouyi, began as a manual for divining with yarrow stalks: each of its sixty-four hexagrams, figures of six broken or unbroken lines, carries a short judgement and a statement for each line, terse images of journeys, marriages, battles and sacrifices. Its core probably took shape at the Western Zhou court. In the late Warring States and early Han, commentators added the Ten Wings, which read the lines as yin and yang, the hexagrams as stages of cosmic transformation, and the book as a guide for the sage to act in harmony with the times. Made the first of the Five Classics under the Han, it attracted more commentary than any other Chinese book, from Wang Bi's metaphysics to Cheng Yi's ethics and Zhu Xi's return to divination, and it travelled to Korea, Japan and, from the seventeenth century, Europe, where Leibniz saw binary arithmetic in its diagrams.

title: Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
creator: Confucius
description: The Chunqiu records, in entries of a few characters each, the events of the state of Lu over 242 years: accessions, deaths, treaties, battles and eclipses. Mencius claimed that Confucius made it, and that wrongdoers trembled at its verdicts, so it was read as a coded moral history in which the choice of a word passed judgement. Three commentaries grew up around it, the narrative Zuozhuan and the question-and-answer Gongyang and Guliang; Dong Zhongshu built his political theory on the Gongyang. Modern scholars doubt that Confucius had much hand in it, but it remained one of the Five Classics and gave its name to the Spring and Autumn period.

title: Analects (Lunyu)
creator: Confucius
location: Lu and other states; received text fixed in the Han
description: The Analects is a collection of about five hundred brief passages in twenty 'books', mostly sayings of Confucius and exchanges with his students, compiled by successive generations of disciples. It sketches the exemplary person (junzi), who loves learning, practises ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety), serves parents with filial piety and governs by moral example; in one famous saying the Master describes his own life as a progression from setting his heart on learning at fifteen to following his heart's desire without transgressing at seventy. Scholars debate how the layers of the text were formed; a version on bamboo slips from a Han tomb at Dingzhou (buried 55 BC) is among the earliest witnesses. The Analects was memorised by schoolchildren throughout East Asia for two millennia, became one of Zhu Xi's Four Books, and is the most influential text on ethics in the region.

title: Mozi
creator: Mozi
description: The Mozi survives in fifty-three of an original seventy-one chapters, written by Mozi's followers over several generations. Its core consists of ten doctrines, each in up to three versions that may reflect rival factions: elevating the worthy, conforming upward, impartial care, condemning offensive war, frugal use, frugal funerals, Heaven's intent, explaining ghosts, condemning music and condemning fatalism. The essays argue methodically, appealing to the precedents of the sage-kings, the evidence of ordinary people's eyes and ears, and benefit to the people. Further chapters record dialogues and describe techniques for defending cities. Long neglected, the book was edited by Qing scholars, especially Sun Yirang, and modern readers have compared its ethics to utilitarianism.

year: c. 4th century BC (earliest manuscript c. 300 BC)
title: Daodejing
creator: Laozi
location: China; earliest witness from the Guodian tomb, Hubei
description: The Daodejing ('Classic of the Way and its Power'), also called the Laozi, opens with the claim that the Dao that can be spoken of is not the constant Dao. In compressed, rhythmic chapters it describes the Dao as an empty, generative source, like a valley or a mother, and recommends that rulers and individuals practise wuwei, acting without forcing, so that things order themselves; water, which yields yet wears away stone, is its emblem. Its date and authorship are debated: the Guodian bamboo manuscripts of about 300 BC contain about two-fifths of the text in a different order, and the two Mawangdui silk copies of the early Han place the 'De' part first. The text has been read as political strategy, mystical philosophy, a manual of self-cultivation and Daoist scripture, and it is among the most translated books in the world.

title: Hui Shi's Ten Theses
creator: Hui Shi
description: The final chapter of the Zhuangzi, 'All Under Heaven', a Han-era survey of the schools, lists ten theses of Hui Shi: the greatest has nothing outside it and the smallest nothing inside it; heaven is as low as earth; the sun at noon is setting; one sets off for Yue today and arrived yesterday; and finally, love all things, for heaven and earth are one body. It also lists the debaters' paradoxes, such as that an egg has feathers. The text gives no arguments, and scholars reconstruct them as reflections on the relativity of spatial and temporal distinctions. Short as it is, the passage is our main evidence for the ideas of the most important early Chinese logician.

title: Guodian Laozi
creator: Laozi
location: Tomb 1, Guodian, Jingmen, Hubei; Hubei Provincial Museum
description: In 1993 archaeologists excavating a Chu tomb at Guodian in Hubei found about eight hundred bamboo slips with writings sealed around 300 BC. Among them were three bundles containing passages that correspond to about a third to two-fifths of the received Daodejing, in a different order and without some of its anti-Confucian lines, together with a previously unknown cosmogony, 'The Great One Gave Birth to Water', and many Confucian essays possibly related to Zisi. The find showed that Laozi sayings circulated in the fourth century BC, but also that the book was still taking shape, sparking intense debate about its formation. The other Guodian texts have transformed the study of Confucianism between Confucius and Mencius.

title: Mohist Canons
creator: Mozi
description: Six chapters of the Mozi, the Canons with their Explanations and the Greater and Lesser Selections, were written by later Mohists in the third century BC, not by Mozi himself. They define terms such as knowledge, benefit, duration and space, distinguish kinds of names, and analyse argument by analogy; other entries describe the pinhole image, plane mirrors and the lever. Badly corrupted in transmission, they became readable only after Qing and twentieth-century reconstruction, notably by A. C. Graham, and are now recognised as the high point of ancient Chinese logic and science.

title: Mencius (Mengzi)
creator: Mencius
description: The Mencius, in seven books each divided in two, records the philosopher's audiences with rulers, debates with rivals and sayings; it may have been compiled by his disciples, perhaps with his participation. It contains the classic arguments for the goodness of human nature: anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm and compassion, the 'sprout' of humaneness. Mencius debates the philosopher Gaozi on whether nature is like water that can flow either way, mocks the farmer of Song who pulled his sprouts to help them grow, and justifies removing a tyrant. Zhu Xi made it one of the Four Books, and its political ideas were cited by reformers and critics of autocracy into the modern age.

title: Discussion on Making All Things Equal (Qiwulun)
creator: Zhuangzi
description: The second of the Inner Chapters begins with a sage who has 'lost himself' and hears the piping of heaven, and proceeds through a dense argument about how every judgement of right and wrong depends on a viewpoint, so that Confucians and Mohists affirm what the other denies. Zhuangzi recommends a 'clarity' that follows things as they are rather than taking sides, and plays with logical puzzles of the School of Names. It ends with Zhuang Zhou dreaming he is a butterfly and, on waking, wondering whether he is a butterfly dreaming he is Zhuang Zhou. The chapter is one of the most discussed texts in Chinese philosophy and has been compared to Pyrrhonian scepticism and to relativism.

title: Zhuangzi
creator: Zhuangzi
location: China; arranged by Guo Xiang c. 300 AD
description: The Zhuangzi opens with a giant fish that becomes a bird flying ninety thousand li, mocked by a cicada and a dove, and goes on to unsettle every fixed standpoint: the cook Ding carves an ox effortlessly by following its natural joints, the useless tree survives because no carpenter wants it, and Zhuangzi drums on a pot after his wife's death. The Inner Chapters are generally ascribed to Zhuangzi or his close circle; the Outer and Miscellaneous Chapters contain material by Primitivists, Yangists, syncretists and others. Guo Xiang's edition of about 300 AD fixed the received text. The book is both a philosophical masterpiece and one of the great works of Chinese prose, and it shaped Xuanxue, Chan Buddhism, landscape painting and poetry.

title: White Horse Dialogue (Baima lun)
creator: Gongsun Long
location: State of Zhao; preserved in the Gongsun Longzi
description: The most famous chapter of the surviving Gongsun Longzi is a dialogue between an objector and a defender of the thesis that a white horse is not a horse. The defender argues that 'horse' names a shape and 'white' a colour, that if you ask for a horse a yellow or black one will do but not if you ask for a white horse, and so the two names cannot be the same. Interpreters have read the argument as a point about the logic of mass nouns, about classes and their members, about the meanings of compound terms, or as pure sophistry. Some scholars think the text was reworked after Gongsun Long's time. It is the best-known product of the School of Names and a touchstone in the debate over whether early China had logic.

title: Great Commentary (Xici zhuan)
creator: Authors of the Book of Changes
location: China; a version is among the Mawangdui silk manuscripts
description: The Xici, or Appended Statements, is a two-part essay attached to the Book of Changes. It explains how the sages created the trigrams by observing heaven, earth and animals, how divination works, and how the hexagrams model the ceaseless 'production and reproduction' of the world. Its formulas, that the alternation of yin and yang is called the Dao and that the Changes has the Great Ultimate (taiji) which produces the two modes, became the starting point for Zhou Dunyi's diagram and much of Neo-Confucian cosmology. A version slightly different from the received text was found among the Mawangdui silk manuscripts buried in 168 BC, showing that the commentary was circulating in the early Han.

title: Xunzi
creator: Xunzi
description: Unlike earlier Chinese texts, the Xunzi consists mainly of extended essays, many probably written by Xunzi himself. 'An Exhortation to Learning' opens with the image of indigo blue that is bluer than the plant it comes from; 'A Discussion of Heaven' treats heaven as the regular course of nature indifferent to human pleas; 'Rectifying Names' analyses how names are fixed by convention; 'Dispelling Obsession' warns against minds fixed on one side of a question; and the chapter claiming that human nature is bad argues that goodness is the product of deliberate effort. Liu Xiang edited the text in the first century BC and Yang Liang wrote its first commentary in 818. Long overshadowed by the Mencius, it is now valued as the most systematic work of classical Confucianism.

title: Human Nature Is Bad (Xing'e)
creator: Xunzi
description: In this chapter Xunzi argues that human beings are born loving profit and envying others, so that following their nature leads to strife; goodness is the result of wei, deliberate effort, as a warped board must be steamed and pressed to become straight. The sages created ritual and moral norms through such effort, and ordinary people can become sages by accumulating it. He examines Mencius's claims point by point. Although Neo-Confucians rejected it as heterodox, the chapter is one of the classic statements of the view that morality is a human construction, and it remains central to debates on Confucian ethics.

title: Han Feizi
creator: Han Fei
description: The Han Feizi collects essays mostly attributed to Han Fei, though some are probably by others. It argues that rulers can rely neither on sages nor on moral persuasion; they must publish clear laws, attach certain rewards and punishments to them, keep officials in check by comparing their words with their results, and hide their own preferences so that no minister can manipulate them. Han Fei illustrates his points with a store of anecdotes, among them the man who sold a spear that could pierce any shield and a shield that no spear could pierce, the origin of the Chinese word for contradiction. Chapters explaining and illustrating the Laozi give Daoist wuwei a political reading. Qin's First Emperor admired the book, and despite official condemnation it remained required reading for statesmen.

title: Great Learning (Daxue)
creator: Compilers of the Book of Rites
type: Classical essay (chapter of the Book of Rites)
description: The Great Learning is a brief chapter of the Book of Rites, traditionally attributed to Confucius's disciple Zengzi, an attribution modern scholars doubt. It sets out a chain of eight steps: investigating things, extending knowledge, making the will sincere, rectifying the mind, cultivating the person, regulating the family, governing the state and bringing peace to all under heaven. Zhu Xi rearranged the text, added a passage of his own on the investigation of things, and placed it first among the Four Books as the framework of learning. Wang Yangming insisted on the older text and reread its key terms, so arguments over this short essay defined the split between the Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools, and its eight steps were memorised across East Asia.

title: Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong)
creator: Compilers of the Book of Rites
type: Classical essay (chapter of the Book of Rites)
description: The Zhongyong, traditionally attributed to Confucius's grandson Zisi, opens by declaring that what Heaven confers is called human nature, following that nature is called the Way, and cultivating the Way is called teaching. It describes a state of equilibrium before emotions arise and harmony when they arise in due measure, and makes sincerity, being true to oneself, the force by which the sage forms a triad with heaven and earth. Song Neo-Confucians valued it as the most metaphysical Confucian text and Zhu Xi made it the culminating book of the Four Books; it was also read closely by Buddhists, and in the West it has been translated as The Doctrine of the Mean or Focusing the Familiar.

title: Mawangdui Silk Manuscripts of the Laozi
creator: Laozi
description: Tomb 3 at Mawangdui near Changsha, the burial of a son of the Marquis of Dai sealed in 168 BC, contained a library of texts written on silk, among them two complete copies of the Laozi, known as A and B, together with versions of the Book of Changes and texts associated with Huang-Lao thought. Both Laozi copies reverse the received order of the book's two halves and differ in many readings from the version transmitted by Wang Bi. Discovered in 1973 and published soon after, they became the basis of a new wave of translations and reopened questions about how the classics were transmitted.

title: Huainanzi
creator: Liu An
location: Court of Huainan; presented to Emperor Wu
description: The Huainanzi ('Masters of Huainan') was written by scholars at the court of Liu An, King of Huainan, and presented to Emperor Wu in 139 BC. Its chapters move from the origin of the cosmos out of formless undifferentiation, through astronomy, topography and the seasonal ordinances, to human nature, military strategy, government and the uses of history, ending with a summary of the whole. It offers the ruler a comprehensive guide to ordering the world in tune with the Dao, drawing on the Laozi and Zhuangzi but also on Confucian, Mohist and Legalist sources. It is the most complete statement of early Han Huang-Lao thought and a treasure house of early Chinese myth, including the story of the old man at the frontier who lost his horse.

title: Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu fanlu)
creator: Dong Zhongshu
description: The Chunqiu fanlu consists of eighty-two chapters, three of them lost, attributed to Dong Zhongshu, though scholars think parts were written by his followers in later centuries. The first section interprets the Spring and Autumn Annals in the Gongyang tradition, finding in its wording Confucius's judgements on rulers; the rest develops a cosmology in which Heaven, Earth and humanity correspond, the ruler links the three as the character for king (wang) links three horizontal strokes, yin and yang and the Five Phases govern the seasons and the state, and natural anomalies signal Heaven's displeasure. The book became the main source for Han imperial Confucianism and for later theories of the mandate of Heaven.

title: Book of Rites (Liji)
creator: Compilers of the Book of Rites
description: The Liji collects writings by Confucian ritual specialists of the late Warring States and Han, ranging from detailed rules of mourning and etiquette to essays on the meaning of ritual, the role of music in shaping emotion, and the ideal society. The chapter 'The Conveyance of Rites' (Liyun) describes an age of Great Unity in which the world was shared by all, a passage Kang Youwei took as his utopian programme. Compiled in the Former Han and associated with Dai Sheng, it became one of the Five Classics, and two of its chapters, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, were later raised to independent canonical status.

title: Discourses Weighed in the Balance (Lunheng)
creator: Wang Chong
description: Wang Chong wrote the Lunheng over many years as a 'balance' to weigh claims. He argues that Heaven is not a purposive being and does not send portents in response to human conduct, that thunder is not Heaven's anger, that the dead do not become ghosts because the vital fluids that animated them disperse, and that fate, not merit, determines success. He criticised Confucius and Mencius where he found their reasoning faulty and pointed out exaggerations in the classics. The book was little valued in imperial times, but twentieth-century scholars hailed it as an early triumph of naturalism and critical thinking.

title: Commentary on the Laozi
creator: Wang Bi
description: Written when Wang Bi was barely twenty, the commentary reads the Laozi as a single coherent argument: all things that have form and name arise from wu, the formless and nameless, which is the 'root' to which the ruler must hold in order to govern without imposing. Wang draws out the political consequences, that a ruler who holds the One allows the many to settle themselves, and ties the text to his reading of the Book of Changes. His essay Outline of the Laozi accompanies it. The version of the Daodejing transmitted with his commentary became the standard text, and his interpretation remains one of the two classical readings of the book, alongside that of Heshang Gong.

title: Outline of the Book of Changes (Zhouyi lüeli)
creator: Wang Bi
description: Wang Bi wrote a commentary on the Book of Changes and this accompanying outline, which swept away the numerological and omen-based interpretation of the Han. He argued that each hexagram captures a single situation, governed by one ruling line, and that words exist to explain images and images to express meaning, so the interpreter, like the fisherman who forgets the trap once he has the fish (an image from the Zhuangzi), should not cling to them. Wang Bi's commentary, completed by Han Kangbo, became the officially recognised one in the Tang, and his principle of 'getting the meaning and forgetting the words' influenced later Chinese hermeneutics and Buddhist readings of scripture.

title: Commentary on the Zhuangzi
creator: Guo Xiang
description: Guo Xiang reduced the fifty-two-chapter Zhuangzi then in circulation to thirty-three, cutting material he considered spurious, and wrote a running commentary, probably building on the lost work of Xiang Xiu. In it he denies that there is any creator, Dao or nothingness from which things come: each thing is 'self-so' and transforms on its own, and contentment lies in fulfilling one's allotted nature, whether one is a great bird or a small one. The sage, he argued, can be fully engaged in affairs while remaining inwardly free. The commentary fixed the text that all later readers used and was a major source of Xuanxue and of Chinese Buddhist thought.

title: Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra (Fahua xuanyi)
creator: Zhiyi
location: Jade Spring Monastery, Jingzhou; recorded by Guanding
description: Lectured in 593 and written down by Guanding, the Fahua xuanyi expounds the five characters of the Lotus Sutra's title at enormous length, using them to set out the Tiantai system: the 'five periods and eight teachings' that arrange the Buddha's sermons into a progression culminating in the Lotus, and the idea that the 'wonderful dharma' is the perfect, all-inclusive truth beyond relative distinctions. This scheme of doctrinal classification (panjiao) was one of the great achievements of Chinese Buddhism, a way of reconciling a vast and contradictory scriptural inheritance, and was adopted in Japan and Korea.

title: Great Calming and Contemplation (Mohe zhiguan)
creator: Zhiyi
location: Jade Spring Monastery, Jingzhou; recorded by Guanding
description: The Mohe zhiguan was delivered as lectures in 594 at Yuquan monastery and edited by Zhiyi's disciple Guanding. It lays out a complete path of practice, the four kinds of samādhi, preparatory disciplines and ten modes of contemplating objects such as the aggregates, illness, karma and demons, grounded in the teaching that the mind in each moment contains all three thousand realms of existence and that every phenomenon is at once empty, provisional and the middle. With the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra and the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra it forms the three great works of Tiantai. It became the core meditative text of Japanese Tendai on Mount Hiei.

title: Seventeen-article Constitution (Jūshichijō kenpō)
creator: Prince Shōtoku
location: Asuka, Yamato; preserved in the Nihon shoki (720)
description: The Nihon shoki dates this text to 604 and credits it to Prince Shōtoku. It is not a constitution in the modern sense but a set of moral precepts for officials: it opens by declaring harmony to be precious, urges reverence for the Three Treasures of Buddhism, obedience to imperial commands, decorum, impartial judgement of lawsuits, the appointment of worthy officials and consultation on important matters rather than deciding alone. Its language draws on the Analects, the Book of Rites, Legalist texts and Buddhist sutras. Whether it was written by Shōtoku, by his court, or by the compilers of the Nihon shoki is debated. It has been invoked ever since as the founding statement of Japanese political ethics.

title: Commentaries on the Three Sutras (Sangyō gisho)
creator: Prince Shōtoku
location: Ikaruga, Yamato; manuscript of the Lotus commentary in the Imperial Household collection
description: Tradition credits Prince Shōtoku with commentaries on three Mahāyāna sutras: the Lotus Sutra, the Śrīmālā Sutra, in which a laywoman queen expounds the dharma, and the Vimalakīrti Sutra, whose hero is a lay bodhisattva. The choice of sutras centred on lay figures suited a lay ruler. The commentaries draw heavily on Chinese works of the Liang dynasty, and whether Shōtoku wrote them or they were brought from China or compiled by his court is debated; a four-scroll manuscript of the Lotus commentary, Hokke gisho, long kept at Hōryū-ji and now in the Imperial collection, is claimed to be in his hand. They stand at the beginning of Japanese Buddhist scholarship.

title: Ten Approaches to the Reconciliation of Doctrinal Controversy (Simmun hwajaeng non)
creator: Wonhyo
description: In this treatise, now surviving only in fragments discovered on woodblocks at Haeinsa, Wonhyo took up ten disputed questions of his time, such as whether all beings possess buddha-nature, whether emptiness and existence conflict, and whether the self and the dharmas are real, and showed that each side was correct from its own standpoint and mistaken only in denying the other. The method of hwajaeng, harmonising disputes, made his work a touchstone for later Korean Buddhists, and modern scholars have taken it as the distinctive character of Korean Buddhism, though how far it differs from Chinese doctrinal classification is debated.

title: Diagram of the Dharma Realm of the One Vehicle of Hwaeom (Hwaeom ilseung beopgye do)
creator: Uisang
location: Tang China (Zhixiang monastery, Mount Zhongnan); presented to Zhiyan
description: Uisang composed this work in 668 while studying with Zhiyan in China and presented it to his teacher shortly before Zhiyan's death. It is a poem of thirty lines of seven characters, arranged on a single red line that winds through a square grid in fifty-four turns, beginning and ending at the centre with the character for dharma and the character for Buddha. Its verses state that the dharma-nature is perfectly interfused, that one is in all and all is in one, and that a single mote of dust contains the ten directions. Uisang added an explanatory commentary. Recited and copied in Korean monasteries ever since, the diagram is the founding document of Korean Hwaeom and a striking union of poetry, image and philosophy.

title: Commentary on the Awakening of Faith (Daeseung gisillon so)
creator: Wonhyo
description: The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, a sixth-century treatise probably composed in China, teaches that one mind has two aspects, suchness and arising-and-ceasing, and so unites the doctrines of buddha-nature and of the storehouse consciousness. Wonhyo wrote two commentaries on it, the Gisillon so and the Byeolgi, arguing that the text resolves the conflict between Madhyamaka emptiness and Yogācāra analysis, which are like the two sides of one coin. Fazang drew on Wonhyo's work in his own celebrated commentary, and Wonhyo's was among the 'three great commentaries' on the treatise in East Asia. It is the clearest statement of the one-mind philosophy that underlies his whole work.

title: Treatise on the Five Teachings of Huayan (Huayan wujiao zhang)
creator: Fazang
description: In this treatise Fazang ranks the Buddhist teachings into five levels, from the Hīnayāna through early and advanced Mahāyāna and the sudden teaching to the perfect teaching of the Avatamsaka Sutra, and expounds the latter's metaphysics: the six characteristics of whole and part, the ten mysterious gates of dependent origination, and the interpenetration of all things in the dharma-realm. It gave Huayan its definitive doctrinal form, was studied in Korean Hwaeom and Japanese Kegon, and is one of the most demanding works of East Asian Buddhist philosophy.

title: Exposition of the Vajrasamādhi Sutra (Geumgang sammaegyeong non)
creator: Wonhyo
description: The Vajrasamādhi Sutra was probably composed in East Asia in the seventh century, and some scholars argue it was written in Silla itself. According to Wonhyo's biography in the Song Biographies of Eminent Monks, a dragon king gave the sutra to the Silla court and only Wonhyo could explain it; he lectured on it riding on an ox, writing his commentary between its horns. Uniquely for a commentary, it was given the title non, 'treatise', normally reserved for works by bodhisattvas. Wonhyo uses the sutra to integrate meditation with doctrine around the theme of the 'contemplation practice of a single taste'. It is often considered his most mature work.

title: Treatise on the Golden Lion (Jin shizi zhang)
creator: Fazang
description: According to tradition, when Empress Wu Zetian found the Huayan teaching hard to follow, Fazang pointed to a golden lion guarding the palace. The gold stands for principle, emptiness without fixed nature, and the lion shape for phenomena arising through conditions; neither exists without the other, and every hair of the lion contains the whole lion and all its other hairs. In ten brief sections the essay runs through the main Huayan doctrines, the six characteristics, the ten mysteries and the interpenetration of principle and phenomena. Its brevity made it the most widely read introduction to Huayan, and Song Neo-Confucians absorbed its relation of one principle and many things.

title: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (Liuzu tanjing)
creator: Huineng
description: The Platform Sutra presents itself as Huineng's sermon from a platform at Dafan temple in Shaozhou, beginning with his autobiography: the illiterate woodcutter, the verse contest with Shenxiu, and the secret transmission of the robe. It teaches that the original nature is pure, that meditation and wisdom are one as a lamp and its light, and that awakening is sudden. It is the only Chinese Buddhist text to be called a sutra, a title otherwise reserved for words of the Buddha. The earliest text, found at Dunhuang, dates from around 780 and shows the influence of Shenhui's campaign for Southern Chan; later editions, especially Zongbao's of 1291, expanded it greatly. It became the founding scripture of Chan, Seon and Zen.

title: Indications of the Goals of the Three Teachings (Sangō shiiki)
creator: Kūkai
description: Written in elegant Chinese parallel prose when Kūkai was twenty-four, the Sangō shiiki explained his decision to abandon a Confucian career. A prodigal youth is lectured in turn by a Confucian gentleman, who recommends loyalty, filial piety and learning; by a Daoist recluse, who recommends the arts of immortality; and by a ragged Buddhist mendicant, modelled on Kūkai himself, who shows that all things are impermanent and that the bodhisattva path surpasses the others. It is the first work in Japan to compare the three teachings and an early masterpiece of Japanese writing in Chinese; an autograph of its earlier draft, the Rōko shiiki, survives at Kongōbu-ji on Mount Kōya.

title: On the Origin of the Way (Yuan Dao)
creator: Han Yu
description: In Yuan Dao Han Yu defines the Way by its Confucian content, humaneness and righteousness, and attacks Buddhism and Daoism for withdrawing from family and state and for producing idle monks who live on others' labour. He quotes the Great Learning, then little regarded, to show that the Confucian path joins inner cultivation to ordering the world, and claims that the true Way was handed down from the sage-kings Yao and Shun through King Wen and the Duke of Zhou to Confucius and Mencius, after which it was lost. Song Neo-Confucians adopted this idea of the transmission of the Way (daotong) and placed themselves at its revival.

title: Attaining Enlightenment in This Very Body (Sokushin jōbutsu gi)
creator: Kūkai
description: In this short treatise Kūkai defends the central claim of Shingon: buddhahood is not reached after countless lifetimes but can be realised 'in this very body'. He explains it through a verse of eight lines, arguing that the six great elements, earth, water, fire, wind, space and consciousness, constitute both the Buddha and all beings and interpenetrate without obstruction; that the four kinds of mandala express this reality; and that the 'three mysteries' of body, speech and mind, practised through mudrā, mantra and meditation, unite the practitioner with Mahāvairocana. With his works on the meanings of sound and of the syllable 'hūṃ', it forms the core of Kūkai's philosophy of language and embodiment.

title: Ten Stages of Mind (Jūjūshinron)
creator: Kūkai
description: In 830 Emperor Junna asked the Buddhist schools to submit summaries of their doctrines, and Kūkai responded with the ten-fascicle Himitsu mandara jūjūshinron and its abridgement, the Precious Key to the Secret Treasury (Hizō hōyaku). The ten stages lead from the mind that, like a goat, knows only food and sex, through the ethical mind awakened by Confucianism and the mind seeking heaven, to the Hīnayāna, Yogācāra, Mādhyamaka, Tendai and Kegon schools, and finally to the esoteric mind of Shingon, which contains all the others. Each lower stage is a partial truth rather than an error. The work is both a doctrinal classification in the tradition of Tiantai and Huayan and the first systematic comparative philosophy written in Japan.

title: Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu)
creator: Zhou Dunyi
description: The Tongshu, also known as Yi Tongshu, is a series of brief chapters that develop the ethical side of Zhou Dunyi's cosmology. Sincerity (cheng), he argues, is the foundation of the sage and the source of the five constant virtues; it is quiescent and without action, yet at the subtle point where thought first stirs, good and evil divide. Sagehood can be learned, and its key is having 'no desire'. The text joined the language of the Book of Changes to the Doctrine of the Mean and helped set the agenda for the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi.

title: Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu shuo)
creator: Zhou Dunyi
description: Zhou Dunyi's short text explains a diagram of concentric circles and linked shapes, probably adapted from a Daoist chart, and opens with the phrase 'Non-polar and yet Supreme Polarity' (wuji er taiji). Movement and stillness of the Supreme Ultimate produce yang and yin, which transform into the Five Phases, and their union produces the myriad things and human beings, the most spiritually responsive of them; the sage settles himself with the mean, correctness, humaneness and righteousness, and makes stillness primary. Zhu Xi placed it at the head of his anthology Reflections on Things at Hand. Its opening words provoked a famous debate between Zhu Xi and Lu Jiuyuan over whether 'non-polar' betrayed a Daoist source.

title: Western Inscription (Ximing)
creator: Zhang Zai
location: Study of Zhang Zai, Hengqu, Shaanxi
description: Zhang Zai inscribed two short texts on the walls of his study; the western one, originally titled 'Correcting Obstinacy', became one of the most loved texts of Neo-Confucianism. It begins by calling Heaven father and Earth mother and the self a small being dwelling in their midst, and from this draws an ethic of universal kinship: all people are siblings and all things companions; caring for the old and orphaned is serving one's parents; and, at its close, living means following and serving, and death is peace. Cheng Yi defended it against the charge of Mohist impartial love by formulating the principle that 'principle is one but its manifestations are many', and Zhu Xi and Korean scholars wrote commentaries on it.

title: Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng)
creator: Zhang Zai
description: In the Zhengmeng Zhang Zai sets out his systematic thought in seventeen sections. All things are condensations of qi, which in its dispersed state is the Great Void, so that being and void are two states of one stuff, and Buddhist and Daoist claims that the world arises from emptiness are mistaken. The Great Harmony is the Dao; human beings have both a heavenly nature and a physical nature, and learning transforms the latter. The Western Inscription is drawn from its final section. The book was later the main inspiration for Wang Fuzhi, whose commentary on it is one of his chief works, and for Korean thinkers who stressed qi.

title: On Understanding Humaneness (Shiren pian)
creator: Cheng Hao
location: Song China; preserved in the Recorded Sayings of the two Chengs
description: This short passage, recorded by Cheng Hao's disciple Lü Dalin, became the classic statement of the elder Cheng's thought. One who is humane forms one body with heaven, earth and all things; righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faithfulness are all aspects of this humaneness. Once one has understood it, one needs only to preserve it with sincerity and reverence, without anxious searching or forcing. Cheng Hao elsewhere compares lack of humaneness to paralysis of the limbs, which do not feel as part of oneself. The text was a touchstone for later scholars of the School of Mind and is often contrasted with Cheng Yi's emphasis on investigation.

title: Commentary on the Book of Changes (Yichuan yizhuan)
creator: Cheng Yi
description: Cheng Yi worked on his commentary to the Book of Changes for decades and completed its preface in 1099, during his political exile in Fuzhou. Discarding numerology, he read each hexagram as a situation in human affairs, in which the cultivated person discerns the principle of the moment and responds rightly. The preface states one of the central formulas of Neo-Confucianism: substance and function come from one source, and there is no gap between the manifest and the hidden. Zhu Xi supplemented it with his own commentary that restored the divinatory dimension, and the two together were official for the Ming examinations.

title: Surviving Works of the Chengs of Henan (Henan Chengshi yishu)
creator: Cheng Yi
description: After the deaths of Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, their disciples circulated notes of their conversations. Zhu Xi gathered these into the Yishu (Surviving Works) of twenty-five chapters in 1168, later adding a supplement. Many sayings are attributed simply to 'the master', so distinguishing the brothers' views has been a perennial scholarly problem. Here appear the Chengs' famous statements that 'nature is principle', that cultivation requires reverence and learning requires the extension of knowledge, and that principle is one while its manifestations are many. The collection was the main source from which Zhu Xi built his system and the model for the genre of Neo-Confucian recorded sayings.

title: Family Rituals (Zhuzi jiali)
creator: Zhu Xi
description: Zhu Xi compiled the Family Rituals to give ordinary gentry households a simplified, practical version of ancient ritual, adapted from Sima Guang and others. It covers the ancestral hall, coming-of-age capping, weddings, funerals and mourning grades, and ancestral sacrifices. The manuscript was reportedly stolen and reappeared only after Zhu's death, which later scholars used to question its authenticity, though most now accept it as substantially his. Through official promotion it shaped family life in Ming and Qing China, and above all in Joseon Korea, where its funeral and ancestral rites became the norm of elite society and the subject of fierce controversies.

title: Reflections on Things at Hand (Jinsilu)
creator: Zhu Xi
location: Cold Spring Study, Fujian; compiled with Lü Zuqian
description: In 1175 Lü Zuqian visited Zhu Xi at his retreat in Fujian, and in ten days the two friends selected passages from the four Northern Song masters and arranged them in fourteen chapters, from the substance of the Way through learning, self-cultivation and family life to government and the critique of heterodoxy. The title comes from the Analects, where reflecting on things at hand is called the method of humaneness. Zhu meant it as a ladder to the Four Books. It became the standard introduction to Neo-Confucianism, was used across Korea and Japan with numerous commentaries, and in Wing-tsit Chan's English translation remains the classic entry point to the school.

title: Goose Lake Debate and Letters of Lu Jiuyuan
creator: Lu Jiuyuan
location: Jiangxi; collected in the Complete Works of Lu Xiangshan
description: Lu Jiuyuan wrote no treatise; his thought survives in letters, poems, lectures and recorded sayings gathered after his death into the Complete Works of Lu Xiangshan. At the Goose Lake Temple in 1175 he and his brother recited poems contrasting their 'simple and easy' method of establishing the original mind with Zhu Xi's 'fragmented' study of texts. In letters of 1188–89 he argued with Zhu over the opening of Zhou Dunyi's diagram, claiming that 'non-polar' was Daoist. The sayings contain his declaration that the universe is his mind. These materials define the Lu side of the greatest debate in Neo-Confucianism.

title: Collected Commentaries on the Four Books (Sishu zhangju jizhu)
creator: Zhu Xi
description: Zhu Xi worked on these commentaries for most of his life and first had the four books printed together at Zhangzhou in 1190, continuing to revise the commentary on the Great Learning until days before his death. By grouping the four texts and prescribing the order of reading, first the Great Learning, then the Analects, the Mencius and finally the Doctrine of the Mean, he made them a curriculum, and his glosses read them through his philosophy of principle, nature and the investigation of things. In 1313 the Yuan court made the commentaries the basis of the civil-service examinations, as they remained under the Ming and Qing until 1905; Joseon Korea and Edo Japan took them as standard too. Few works of philosophy have shaped so many lives.

title: Secrets on Cultivating the Mind (Susim gyeol)
creator: Jinul
description: Written in the form of questions and answers, the Susim gyeol explains that the mind of every person is Buddha and that one must look within rather than seek outside. Awakening to this is sudden, like realising one's mistake on waking; but long-accumulated habits remain, so it must be followed by gradual cultivation, as ice that is water by nature still needs time to melt. Jinul describes this cultivation as the balanced practice of samādhi and prajñā, and answers objections from those who think practice unnecessary after awakening. It remains a standard text for Korean monks and lay practitioners and was translated by Robert Buswell.

title: Excerpts from the Dharma Collection with Personal Notes (Beopjip byeolhaeng nok jeoryo byeongip sagi)
creator: Jinul
description: In this major treatise Jinul quotes and comments on the Chinese master Zongmi's comparison of the Chan lineages, accepting his argument that understanding must precede practice and that awakening is sudden while cultivation is gradual. He then goes beyond Zongmi, concluding with Dahui's 'shortcut' method of investigating a hwadu, a critical phrase from a Chan dialogue, as the means to cut through conceptual understanding. The work became part of the Korean monastic curriculum and fixed the Korean Seon synthesis of doctrinal study, gradual cultivation and kanhwa meditation.

title: Teaching, Practice, Faith and Realisation (Kyōgyōshinshō)
creator: Shinran
description: The six-fascicle Kyōgyōshinshō, properly Ken jōdo shinjitsu kyōgyōshō monrui, was begun, according to the True Pure Land tradition, around 1224 in the Kantō and revised until late in Shinran's life. It assembles passages from sutras and from Indian, Chinese and Japanese masters, with Shinran's interpretations, to show that the true teaching is the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the true practice is saying Amida's name, the true faith is the entrusting given by Amida, and the true realisation is birth in the Pure Land and nirvana. Shinran rereads classical Chinese passages so that the agent of faith becomes Amida rather than the believer. An autograph manuscript at Higashi Honganji is a National Treasure. It is the foundational text of Jōdo Shinshū, the largest Buddhist denomination in Japan.

title: Universal Recommendation for Zazen (Fukan zazengi)
creator: Dōgen
description: Dōgen composed the Fukan zazengi soon after returning from China in 1227, to make the practice of zazen available to everyone, and revised it in 1233; the autograph of that version, in elegant Chinese, survives at Eihei-ji and is designated a National Treasure. It explains how to sit, breathe and hold the mind, but also insists that zazen is not a method for attaining awakening: it is 'the dharma gate of ease and joy', the practice-realisation of awakening itself. Recited daily in Sōtō temples, it is the shortest statement of the conviction that runs through all of Dōgen's work.

title: Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Shōbōgenzō)
creator: Dōgen
description: The Shōbōgenzō is a collection of essays, many delivered as talks to Dōgen's monks between 1231 and 1253, that survives in compilations of 75, 12 and later 95 chapters. Written in a Japanese dense with Chinese Buddhist terms, puns and deliberate rereadings of classical phrases, it explores 'Genjōkōan', where to study the self is to forget the self; 'Uji' (being-time), which identifies existence with time; 'Busshō' (buddha-nature), which reads the phrase 'all sentient beings have buddha-nature' as 'all beings are buddha-nature' and identifies buddha-nature with impermanence; and topics of monastic practice. Little studied outside Sōtō for centuries, it was rediscovered by Watsuji Tetsurō in the 1920s and is now recognised as one of the summits of Japanese thought, often compared with Heidegger.

title: Classified Conversations of Master Zhu (Zhuzi yulei)
creator: Zhu Xi
description: Zhu Xi's many students took notes of his answers to their questions over some thirty years, and in 1270 Li Jingde combined the various collections into a single work of 140 chapters arranged by topic: principle and qi, heaven and earth, ghosts and spirits, human nature, learning, the classics, the Song masters, Buddhism and Daoism, history and literature. Lively and colloquial, the conversations show Zhu working out problems, changing his mind and correcting students. They are indispensable for understanding his metaphysics and were studied intensely in Korea, where Yi Hwang and others compiled selections, and in Japan.

title: A Record in Lament of Divergences (Tannishō)
creator: Shinran
description: The Tannishō was written about thirty years after Shinran's death, probably by his disciple Yuien, who 'laments' the divergences from his master's teaching that had arisen among followers. Its first part records sayings of Shinran in vivid Japanese, including his declaration that he does not know whether the nembutsu leads to the Pure Land or to hell, and the paradox that if even good people attain birth, how much more the evil person; the second part corrects specific errors. The fifteenth-century Shin leader Rennyo restricted access to it; rediscovered in the Meiji era by Kiyozawa Manshi, it became one of the most read religious texts of modern Japan and attracted philosophers such as Nishida and Tanabe.

title: Array of Critiques of Buddhism (Bulssi japbyeon)
creator: Jeong Do-jeon
description: In nineteen short chapters Jeong Do-jeon attacks the Buddhist teachings of transmigration, karma, the mind as source of all things, the illusoriness of the world, and the renunciation of family life, using the Cheng-Zhu philosophy of principle and material force: the dispersal of qi at death disproves rebirth; the Buddhists see the mind but not the principle within it; and their withdrawal from human relations destroys the moral order. He also blames the decline of past dynasties on Buddhist patronage. Completed in 1398, the year of his murder, it was published in 1456 and provided the intellectual basis for the Joseon state's long suppression of Buddhism.

title: Instructions for Practical Living (Chuanxi lu)
creator: Wang Yangming
description: The Chuanxi lu, whose title comes from the Analects phrase about practising what one has been taught, was first printed by Wang Yangming's disciple Xue Kan in 1518; further parts added in 1524 and after Wang's death brought it to three books. In lively dialogues Wang argues that there is no principle outside the mind, so that filial piety is not found in one's parents but in one's own mind; that knowing and acting are one, since seeing a beautiful colour already involves liking it; and that liangzhi, the innate knowing of good, is complete in everyone. The text includes his 'Four-Sentence Teaching' on the original substance of mind beyond good and evil, which split his followers. Its English title comes from Wing-tsit Chan's 1963 translation; in Japan, as Denshūroku, it was a favourite of reformers and activists.

title: Inquiry on the Great Learning (Daxue wen)
creator: Wang Yangming
description: Written down by his disciple Qian Dehong just before Wang set out on his final campaign in 1527, the Inquiry on the Great Learning was intended as an introduction to his teaching for new students. Wang explains that the great person regards heaven, earth and all things as one body, as shown when we feel alarm at a child about to fall into a well, pity for a frightened animal or regret at a broken tile, and that self-centred desire obscures this humaneness. 'Investigating things' means correcting the mind's intentions in each affair, and 'extending knowledge' means extending innate knowing. It is the most concise statement of his mature philosophy.

title: Four–Seven Debate Letters (Sadan chiljeong non)
creator: Yi Hwang
location: Andong and Hanyang; letters between Yi Hwang and Gi Dae-seung
description: In 1559 Gi Dae-seung (Gobong), twenty-six years Toegye's junior, questioned a formulation in which Yi Hwang had said that the four beginnings of Mencius (compassion, shame, deference and the sense of right) issue from principle and the seven emotions of the Book of Rites from material force. Gi argued that the four are simply the good portion of the seven and that principle and qi cannot be separated. Over seven years of respectful letters Toegye refined his view: in the four, principle issues and qi follows; in the seven, qi issues and principle rides on it. The exchange, later continued by Yi I and Seong Hon, raised questions about the relation of moral and ordinary emotion that Chinese Neo-Confucians had left untouched, and it defined Korean philosophy for three centuries.

title: Ten Diagrams on Sage Learning (Seonghak sipdo)
creator: Yi Hwang
description: In 1568, at the age of sixty-eight, Yi Hwang presented ten diagrams to the seventeen-year-old King Seonjo, so that the king might keep them before him as a screen or album. Seven derive from earlier Chinese and Korean scholars, among them Zhou Dunyi's diagram of the Supreme Ultimate and the Western Inscription, and three are Toegye's own; each is accompanied by a text and his commentary. They lead from the cosmos through the Great Learning and elementary learning to the relation of mind, nature and feelings, the Four-Seven question and the practice of reverence in daily life. Compact and profound, it is the best-known summary of Korean Neo-Confucianism and was frequently printed in Korea and Japan.

title: Letters to Seong Hon on Principle and Material Force
creator: Yi I
description: In 1572 Seong Hon (Ugye) wrote to his friend Yi I asking whether Toegye's view of the four beginnings and seven emotions was correct. In nine replies Yulgok argued that there is only one way in which feelings arise: material force issues and principle rides upon it. The four beginnings are not a separate source but the good part of the seven emotions; principle is universal and pervasive, while qi is particular and limiting, a formula (igi tong guk) that summed up his philosophy. The letters founded the Giho school of Yulgok's followers, which debated Toegye's Yeongnam school for the rest of the Joseon dynasty.

title: Essentials of the Studies of the Sages (Seonghak jibyo)
creator: Yi I
description: Yi I presented the Seonghak jibyo to King Seonjo in 1575 as a more practical and Korean alternative to the Chinese Extended Meaning of the Great Learning by Zhen Dexiu. In five parts, following the structure of the Great Learning, it gathers passages from the classics and the Song masters with Yulgok's commentary, moving from the ruler's self-cultivation, through the regulation of his family, to governing and the transmission of the Way. It reflects Yulgok's conviction that moral learning must issue in institutional reform, and became a standard text in the education of later Joseon kings.

title: Essential Secrets for Removing Ignorance (Gyeongmong yogyeol)
creator: Yi I
description: Written in 1577 while Yi I was living in Haeju, the Gyeongmong yogyeol was intended for young students who had just begun to learn. In ten chapters it urges them to set their will on becoming sages, to change old habits, to keep their bodies and minds in order, to read the classics in a prescribed sequence, and to serve their parents, conduct funerals and sacrifices, manage the household and deal with others correctly. Simple and practical, it became one of the most widely used primers in Joseon schools, alongside the Elementary Learning. An autograph manuscript with an inkstone associated with Yulgok is preserved at Ojukheon in Gangneung.

title: A Book to Burn (Fenshu)
creator: Li Zhi
description: Li Zhi called this collection A Book to Burn because, he wrote, it was bound to give offence. Published in 1590, it gathers his letters to friends and critics, notably the official Geng Dingxiang, together with essays and poems. In 'On the Childlike Mind' he argues that the genuine mind one has before received doctrines take over is the source of all good writing, and that the classics, compiled from fragments by disciples, cannot be taken as eternal truth; elsewhere he defends the abilities of women and praises vernacular fiction and drama. Banned after his death in 1602 and again under the Qing, it circulated nonetheless, and a sequel, A Book to Keep Hidden, contains his iconoclastic historical judgements.

title: Treatise on the Three Virtues (Santokushō)
creator: Hayashi Razan
description: The Santokushō takes its theme from the Doctrine of the Mean, which names wisdom, humaneness and courage as the three universal virtues, and expounds them in simple Japanese for samurai and other readers who could not read Chinese. Hayashi Razan explains Zhu Xi's teaching that the virtues are principle inherent in the mind and that cultivation requires reverent seriousness, and applies it to the hierarchy of Tokugawa society. Works of this kind, alongside his lectures and his role at the shogunate, did much to make Neo-Confucian vocabulary part of Edo culture, though the dating and attribution of some of Razan's Japanese writings are uncertain.

title: Dialogue with an Old Man (Okina mondō)
creator: Nakae Tōju
description: In the Okina mondō a disciple questions an old teacher on the meaning of learning and the Way. Nakae Tōju answers that filial piety is not only duty to parents but the virtue that unites a person with heaven, earth and the 'Great Lord on High', the source of all life, and that learning means cultivating the mind rather than reading books. Written in plain Japanese and addressed to warriors, farmers and women alike, it adapts Confucian teaching to circumstances, a point Tōju stressed in the idea of acting according to time, place and status. Printed after his death, it made him one of the best-loved Confucians of Japan and an early exponent of Wang Yangming's learning.

title: Outer Commentary on the Book of Changes (Zhouyi waizhuan)
creator: Wang Fuzhi
description: Written during Wang Fuzhi's years of hiding in Hunan, this 'outer' commentary, as opposed to his line-by-line 'inner' commentary, uses the Book of Changes to develop his own philosophy. Against Neo-Confucian talk of a principle prior to things, he insists that the Way exists only in concrete instruments (qi 器), that without the thing there is no Way, and that reality is a continuous process of the vital stuff (qi 氣) giving rise to ever-new forms. Unknown in his lifetime, it was printed in the nineteenth century and has since been read as a culmination of Chinese philosophies of change.

title: Waiting for the Dawn (Mingyi daifang lu)
creator: Huang Zongxi
description: Writing in 1663 after two decades of failed resistance to the Qing, Huang Zongxi set out a plan for a future ruler, the title alluding to a hexagram of the Book of Changes in which light is hidden, waiting to be called on. He argues that the ancients regarded the realm as master and the ruler as guest, but later rulers treated the realm as private property; that law should be for the whole realm, not for the dynasty; that the chief minister should be restored as a check on the throne; and that schools and academies should judge right and wrong for the court. Proposals on land, taxation, the military and eunuchs follow. Banned under the Qing, the book was printed by late Qing reformers as a Chinese charter of democratic ideas.

title: Record of Daily Knowledge (Rizhi lu)
creator: Gu Yanwu
description: Gu Yanwu took his title from the Analects phrase about knowing each day what one lacks. Over some thirty years he recorded findings on the classics, government, economics, geography, rites and language, testing each claim against texts, inscriptions and his own observation during his travels. The notes show his conviction that learning must be grounded in evidence and useful to the world, and they contain his famous distinction between the fall of a dynasty and the fall of 'all under heaven', the moral order for which everyone is responsible. Published in an expanded thirty-two-chapter edition after his death, it was the model for Qing kaozheng scholarship.

title: Records of Ming Scholars (Mingru xue'an)
creator: Huang Zongxi
description: Huang Zongxi's Mingru xue'an surveys more than two hundred Ming thinkers, grouping them by lineage and region, with a critical introduction to each school, a biography of each scholar and excerpts from his writings. It gives special attention to Wang Yangming and his followers, whom Huang divided into regional schools, and ends with his own teacher Liu Zongzhou. Huang aimed to show how each scholar had reached his own insight. The work created the genre of the 'scholarly case' history; Huang began a similar history of Song and Yuan Confucians that was completed by others, and the book remains the starting point for the study of Ming philosophy.

title: The Meaning of Terms in the Analects and Mencius (Gomō jigi)
creator: Itō Jinsai
description: Jinsai drafted the Gomō jigi in 1683 and revised it throughout his life; it was printed in the year of his death. In thirty entries, on terms such as the Way of heaven, fate, the Way, principle, virtue, humaneness, the mind, nature and loyalty, he argues from the Analects and the Mencius that Song scholars had imported Buddhist and Daoist ideas of quiescence and an abstract principle. For Jinsai the universe is a single living, generative qi; the Way is the path of everyday human relations; and humaneness is love. The book anticipated by a century Dai Zhen's similar project in China, and it set the method of 'ancient learning' (kogaku) in Japan.

title: On Reading the Comprehensive Mirror (Du Tongjian lun)
creator: Wang Fuzhi
description: In one of his last works Wang Fuzhi commented, reign by reign, on the events recorded in Sima Guang's Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, from the Warring States to the end of the Five Dynasties. He judges rulers and ministers, but also argues that historical circumstances (shi) shape what is possible, that the abolition of feudal domains under the Qin was a necessary development despite the Qin's wickedness, and that laws suited to one era are unsuitable to another. His fierce distinctions between Chinese and 'barbarians' made the book a resource for anti-Manchu revolutionaries; its sense of historical process has interested modern philosophers of history.

title: Boy's Questions (Dōjimon)
creator: Itō Jinsai
description: The Dōjimon presents Jinsai's teaching as a series of questions from a young student and the master's answers, in three fascicles. It returns to his central themes: that the Analects is the supreme book in the universe, that the Way lies in the everyday relations of ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, sibling and friend, and that humaneness is essentially love and lies close at hand. It insists that learning should cultivate practical virtue rather than speculation on human nature. Published two years after his death, it is the most accessible statement of his mature thought.

title: Distinguishing the Way (Bendō)
creator: Ogyū Sorai
description: In the Bendō and its companion Benmei (Distinguishing Names), both completed in 1717, Sorai attacked Song Neo-Confucians and Itō Jinsai alike for misunderstanding the ancient language of the classics. The Way of the sages, he argued, is a collective name for the rites, music, punishments and government that the early kings invented to pacify the realm; it was not found in nature or in the mind but made, and its purpose is the peace and welfare of the people rather than personal cultivation. Individuals contribute by developing their particular talents in service of that order. The work is the key text of Sorai's school and of what Maruyama Masao read as the separation of politics from ethics in Tokugawa thought.

title: Discourse on Government (Seidan)
creator: Ogyū Sorai
location: Edo; submitted to the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune
description: Written privately for the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune, the Seidan diagnoses the ills of Tokugawa society: samurai living like 'travellers in an inn' in castle towns, dependent on merchants and money, and a population drifting out of control. Sorai proposes returning samurai to the land, strict household registration, sumptuary laws and the reestablishment of institutions in the spirit of the ancient kings. The text circulated in manuscript and was printed only much later. It shows how Sorai's philosophy of the Way as institutions translated into concrete statecraft, and is a key source for Edo social history.

title: The Way of Nature and Labour (Shizen shin'eidō)
creator: Andō Shōeki
location: Hachinohe, Mutsu; manuscript mostly lost in 1923
description: The Shizen shin'eidō survives in a three-fascicle printed version of 1753 and fragments of a manuscript of about a hundred fascicles, most of which was destroyed in the fire after the 1923 earthquake. Shōeki describes nature as a self-moving process of advancing and retreating qi, in which men and women, heaven and earth, form complementary pairs without hierarchy. In the original 'world of nature' everyone farmed; then sages, Buddhas and rulers created the 'world of law', with its classes and doctrines, in order to eat without working. He prescribes 'direct cultivation' by all. Unknown until 1899, the work has been read as a precursor of anarchism and ecological thought.

title: The Essentials of the Tale of Genji (Shibun yōryō)
creator: Motoori Norinaga
description: In 1763 Norinaga wrote two treatises, the Shibun yōryō on The Tale of Genji and the Isonokami sasamegoto on poetry. Rejecting Buddhist and Confucian readings of Genji as a moral allegory or warning against lust, he argued that the novel's purpose is to make readers know mono no aware, the capacity to be deeply moved by things, and that its characters are judged good or bad by their sensitivity, not by conventional morality. This theory of literature as the expression and cultivation of feeling became one of the cornerstones of Japanese aesthetics and of Norinaga's wider critique of Chinese rationalism.

title: Evidential Study of the Meaning of Terms in the Mencius (Mengzi ziyi shuzheng)
creator: Dai Zhen
description: Completed shortly before his death, this work takes the form of a lexicon of key terms in the Mencius, principle (li), the Way, nature, talent, humaneness and others, each explained through evidence from ancient texts. Dai Zhen argues that principle originally meant the fine pattern within things, discovered by careful examination, not a metaphysical entity implanted in the mind; that desires and feelings are part of human nature and principle is their proper fulfilment; and that Song Confucians, by opposing principle to desire, enabled the powerful to condemn the weak in the name of principle. Little read in his lifetime, it was championed by Zhang Binglin, Liang Qichao and Hu Shi as a precursor of modern humanism.

title: Jehol Diary (Yeolha ilgi)
creator: Bak Ji-won
location: Written after the 1780 embassy to Beijing and Jehol
description: In 1780 Bak Ji-won travelled with a Joseon embassy to congratulate the Qianlong Emperor on his seventieth birthday, going to Beijing and then to the summer palace at Jehol (Rehe, now Chengde). His account, written in a lively, unorthodox classical style, describes Chinese carts, kilns, bricks, markets and buildings, conversations with Chinese scholars and Tibetan lamas, and argues that Korea should learn from the Qing rather than despising them as barbarians. It also contains the satirical tales 'Master Heo' and 'The Tiger's Rebuke'. Its style was condemned by King Jeongjo, but the book became the classic of the Northern Learning school and of Korean travel writing.

title: Commentary on the Kojiki (Kojiki-den)
creator: Motoori Norinaga
description: The Kojiki, compiled in 712, records Japan's myths and early imperial history in a mixture of Chinese characters used for meaning and sound that had become almost unreadable. Motoori Norinaga spent thirty-five years reconstructing its readings in ancient Japanese, word by word, and commenting on every passage. In the introductory essay Naobi no mitama he argued that the Kojiki records the true Way of the gods, received from the sun goddess Amaterasu, which needs no Chinese moralising and can only be accepted, not rationalised. The philology was a monumental scholarly achievement still used today; the theology made the Kojiki a central text of later Shinto nationalism.

title: Design for Good Government (Gyeongse yupyo)
creator: Jeong Yak-yong
description: Originally titled 'Bangnye chobon', the Gyeongse yupyo uses the Rites of Zhou as a model for the complete reorganisation of the Joseon government: the structure of ministries, the examination and appointment of officials, a well-field land system adapted to Korean conditions, fair taxation and military reform. Jeong Yak-yong left it unfinished but it is the most ambitious institutional plan of the Silhak movement. With the Mongmin simseo on local government and the Heumheum sinseo on criminal justice, it forms the trilogy of Dasan's practical writings.

title: Admonitions on Governing the People (Mongmin simseo)
creator: Jeong Yak-yong
description: Written at the end of Jeong Yak-yong's eighteen years of exile in Gangjin, the Mongmin simseo is addressed to the local magistrates who directly governed the Korean people. Its twelve parts, from taking up office to leaving it, cover personal integrity, care for the elderly and destitute, taxes, corvée, justice, rites, the military, public works and famine relief, drawing on Chinese and Korean precedent and on Dasan's own observations of abuses by clerks and officials. Its title calls it the 'heart's book' because the exiled author could only write what he could not carry out. It became a classic of Korean public administration and is still read by officials today.

title: Great Scripture of Eastern Learning (Donggyeong daejeon)
creator: Choe Je-u
location: Gyeongju; compiled and printed by Choe Si-hyeong
description: The Donggyeong daejeon gathers the essays Choe Je-u wrote in classical Chinese between his revelation of 1860 and his arrest, among them 'Discussion of Learning' (Nonhak mun), which explains why his teaching is 'Eastern Learning' rather than Western Learning, and the twenty-one-character incantation. Its central idea is sicheonju, 'bearing the Lord of Heaven within', which implied the equal dignity of every person irrespective of class. His successor Choe Si-hyeong compiled and printed it in 1880, together with the vernacular songs of the Yongdam yusa. It is the scripture of Donghak and a key text of nineteenth-century Korean thought.

title: An Encouragement of Learning (Gakumon no susume)
creator: Fukuzawa Yukichi
description: Fukuzawa Yukichi's series opens with the famous statement that, it is said, heaven does not create one person above or below another, and argues that differences in status come from learning. By learning he meant practical knowledge, reading, writing, arithmetic, geography, physics, economics and ethics, which enables people to stand on their own and so to build an independent nation. Later pamphlets discuss the equality of nations, the duties of citizens, the evils of servility and the role of private initiative. Written in plain Japanese, the series sold, by Fukuzawa's estimate, over three million copies, about one for every ten Japanese, and shaped the values of Meiji education.

title: An Outline of a Theory of Civilization (Bunmeiron no gairyaku)
creator: Fukuzawa Yukichi
description: Fukuzawa's most systematic work describes civilisation as a relative and progressive state, measured by the knowledge and virtue of the whole people rather than by its rulers. Drawing on the historians François Guizot and Henry Thomas Buckle, he argued that Western nations were 'civilised', China and Japan 'half-civilised', and that Japan's traditional imbalance of power, which concentrated authority in the government, had stunted the people's spirit. The goal of civilisation in Japan's present situation, he concluded, was the preservation of national independence. The book is the classic of the Meiji enlightenment and was re-examined in detail by Maruyama Masao.

title: A Study of Confucius as a Reformer (Kongzi gaizhi kao)
creator: Kang Youwei
description: Building on his earlier attack on the Old Text classics as forgeries by the Han scholar Liu Xin, Kang Youwei argued in this book that Confucius, like the other masters of the Warring States, had created an idealised antiquity of sage-kings in order to justify changing the institutions of his own day. Confucius thus became a prophet of progress and a founder of a religion, and Kang read the Gongyang theory of three ages as a forecast of advance toward democracy. Published on the eve of the 1898 reforms, the book was banned and its printing blocks burned; it shook traditional confidence in the classics and opened the way to the 'doubting antiquity' movement of the 1920s.

title: Book of the Great Unity (Datong shu)
creator: Kang Youwei
location: Written partly in exile in India; published posthumously in Shanghai
description: Kang Youwei claimed to have begun this book in 1884 and wrote most of it in Darjeeling around 1901–02; parts were published in 1913 but the whole appeared only in 1935, after his death. Inspired by the Book of Rites' account of an age of Great Unity, Buddhist compassion and Western utopian thought, it surveys the sufferings of humanity and traces them to boundaries: of nations, classes, races, sexes, families, property and species. In the coming age, Kang predicts, these will dissolve: a world parliament will govern, marriage will be replaced by renewable contracts, children raised in public institutions and the dead cremated in public. Mao Zedong cited the book, noting that Kang had not found the road to the Great Unity.

title: On the New Citizen (Xinmin shuo)
creator: Liang Qichao
description: Published serially from 1902 in Liang Qichao's Yokohama journal Xinmin congbao (New Citizen Journal), these essays argued that China's weakness lay less in its government than in its people, who had been subjects of dynasties rather than citizens of a nation. Liang called for public morality, national consciousness, a spirit of adventure, rights and duties, freedom, self-government and progress, drawing on Japanese translations of Western political thought and social Darwinism. Written in a vivid new style, the essays were read by a generation of young Chinese, including Mao Zedong and Hu Shi.

title: An Inquiry into the Good (Zen no kenkyū)
creator: Nishida Kitarō
description: Written while Nishida was teaching in Kanazawa and published in 1911, An Inquiry into the Good begins from pure experience, the direct awareness of, for example, a colour or a sound before one judges that 'I' perceive 'it'. From there Nishida argues that reality is a single self-developing system of consciousness, that the good is the realisation of the self's true personality in unity with that reality, and that religion is the deepest form of this unity, which he linked to God. He drew on William James, Wundt, Hegel and his own Zen practice. Often called the first original work of modern Japanese philosophy, it was widely read by students and remains Nishida's most accessible book.

title: On the Reform of Korean Buddhism (Joseon bulgyo yusin non)
creator: Han Yong-un
description: Written in 1910 and published in 1913, the treatise argues that Buddhism's core values are equality and saving all beings, which accord with modern ideas of freedom and progress, but that Korean Buddhism had decayed in remote mountain monasteries under centuries of Joseon repression. Han calls for modern education of monks, simplified rituals, the relocation of temples to cities, the abolition of superstitious practices, economic self-reliance and, controversially, permission for monks to marry. Influenced by Liang Qichao's writings and by Japanese Buddhist modernisation, it is the founding document of modern Korean Buddhist reform.

title: Outline of the History of Chinese Philosophy (Zhongguo zhexue shi dagang)
creator: Hu Shi
description: Based on Hu Shi's Columbia dissertation and lectures at Peking University, this first volume, covering the period up to the Qin, began not with the legendary sage-kings but with the Book of Odes as historical evidence, and treated Confucius, Mozi, the later Mohists and Zhuangzi as philosophers whose arguments could be analysed and compared with Western logic. It gave special attention to logical method and to the Mohist canons. Cai Yuanpei's preface praised its critical approach. Hu never completed the later volumes, but the book established the discipline of Chinese philosophy in modern universities, and its method was soon followed and challenged by Feng Youlan.

title: Intellectual Trends in the Qing Period (Qingdai xueshu gailun)
creator: Liang Qichao
description: Written in two weeks in 1920 as a preface to another book and published separately the next year, this survey describes Qing learning as a cycle of birth, flourishing, transformation and decline, in which reaction against Ming philosophy led to Gu Yanwu and Huang Zongxi, then to the evidential learning of Dai Zhen and the Qianlong era, and finally to the New Text school of Kang Youwei and Liang himself. He compared the movement to the European Renaissance. The book, translated into English by Immanuel Hsü, shaped the modern understanding of Qing thought for decades.

title: Eastern and Western Cultures and Their Philosophies (Dong-Xi wenhua ji qi zhexue)
creator: Liang Shuming
location: Lectures in Beijing and Jinan; published in Beijing
description: Delivered as lectures in 1920–21 and published in 1921, at the height of the May Fourth attack on tradition, this book argued that cultures differ in their basic orientation of the will: the West presses forward to master nature, China seeks harmony and balance, and India turns back to renounce desire. Each suits a stage of human development, and the world, having reached material sufficiency through Western science, would next need the Confucian attitude, with India's to come later. Drawing on Bergson and Yogācāra Buddhism as well as Confucius and Wang Yangming, it became a bestseller and launched the cultural conservatism later called New Confucianism.

title: Place (Basho)
creator: Nishida Kitarō
location: Tokyo: in the journal Tetsugaku kenkyū
description: Published in 1926 and later included in From the Acting to the Seeing, 'Basho' turned Nishida from the psychology of experience to logic. Aristotle had defined substance as what is a subject and never a predicate; Nishida reverses the perspective and asks about the 'place' in which subjects and predicates, knower and known, are located. Physical things are located in a field of consciousness, which is in turn located in deeper places, until one reaches a place of 'absolute nothingness' that cannot itself be objectified. This logic of basho became the core of Nishida's mature philosophy and the defining idea of the Kyoto School.

title: A History of Chinese Philosophy (Zhongguo zhexue shi)
creator: Feng Youlan
description: Feng Youlan's history, whose first volume appeared in 1931 and second in 1934, divided Chinese philosophy into an 'Age of the Philosophers' up to the early Han and an 'Age of Classical Learning' from Dong Zhongshu to the end of the Qing. Combining careful use of sources with conceptual analysis on Western lines, it treated each thinker's ideas systematically and gave unusual attention to the School of Names, the later Mohists and Neo-Confucian metaphysics. Unlike Hu Shi, Feng accepted traditional dating less critically but went further into philosophical interpretation. Bodde's English translation (1937–53) made it the main source for Western knowledge of the subject for half a century.

title: New Treatise on Consciousness-Only (Xin weishi lun)
creator: Xiong Shili
description: After years of studying Yogācāra Buddhism, Xiong Shili came to reject its theory of seeds and stored consciousness, and in this book, published in classical Chinese in 1932 and in an enlarged vernacular version in 1944, he built his own system. Reality is an original substance that exists only in its functioning, a constant 'closing and opening' that produces the world; the mind that grasps this is the original mind of the Confucians, and the Book of Changes, not Buddhism, expresses it best. His former Buddhist teachers wrote rebuttals, provoking a major debate. The book founded the metaphysical strand of New Confucianism.

title: Climate and Culture (Fūdo)
creator: Watsuji Tetsurō
description: Fūdo grew out of Watsuji's sea voyage to Europe in 1927 and his reading of Heidegger's Being and Time, which he felt neglected the spatial and social dimension of existence. Human beings, he argued, discover themselves through fūdo, the climate and environment in which they live; the cold we feel is not merely a physical state but a way in which we already exist together outside ourselves. He distinguishes three types: the monsoon of South and East Asia, receptive and resigned; the desert, combative and submissive to a single god; and the European meadow, regular and rational, with a special analysis of Japan. The typology has been criticised as essentialist, but the book founded a philosophy of environment and is still widely read.

title: Ethics (Rinrigaku)
creator: Watsuji Tetsurō
description: Watsuji built his ethics on the Japanese word ningen, written with characters meaning 'person' and 'between', to argue that a human being is at once an individual and a member of relationships, and that ethics is the study of the 'betweenness' (aidagara) in which we exist. Individuality arises by negating the community and the community by negating the individual, in a continuing double negation that ultimately expresses emptiness. The volumes trace this structure through family, kin, local community, economy, culture and the state. Its account of the state was criticised after the war and revised by Watsuji; the work is the most systematic ethical philosophy of modern Japan.

title: A New Treatise on Neo-Confucianism (Xin lixue)
creator: Feng Youlan
description: Written while Feng's university had fled the Japanese invasion to the southwest, the Xin lixue 'continues', rather than merely repeats, the Neo-Confucianism of the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi. Using logical analysis influenced by the new realism he had encountered at Columbia, Feng sets out four formal concepts, principle, qi, the substance of the Way and the Great Whole, which say nothing about actual facts but describe what must be the case for anything to exist. The book was followed by works on society, human life and method, including A New Treatise on the Nature of Man, which describes four spheres of life from the natural to that of heaven and earth. Together they form the most ambitious system of Chinese philosophy in the twentieth century.

title: Philosophy as Metanoetics (Zangedō to shite no tetsugaku)
creator: Tanabe Hajime
description: Tanabe delivered the substance of this book as lectures in the autumn of 1944, as Japan's defeat loomed, and published it in 1946. Feeling that he had neither resisted nor rightly guided his nation, he concluded that philosophy itself must undergo zange, repentance or metanoia: reason must recognise its own powerlessness and surrender to an 'other power' that restores it in a new form. Drawing on Shinran's Pure Land faith and on Kant, Hegel and Kierkegaard, he called this 'metanoetics', a philosophy that is not his own work but the action of absolute nothingness through him. The book is a rare example of a philosopher's public self-criticism after the war.

title: Religion and Nothingness (Shūkyō to wa nanika)
creator: Nishitani Keiji
description: The essays collected as Shūkyō to wa nanika ('What is religion?') ask how religion is possible after science and Nietzsche. Nishitani argues that the modern self, which treats everything as an object of its own representation, is underlain by a 'field of nihility' revealed in anxiety and the sense of meaninglessness. Rather than fleeing it, one must pass through it to the 'field of emptiness' (śūnyatā), where self and things are no longer opposed and each appears in its own mode of being, in a circuminsession with all others. He engages Christianity, Eckhart, Nietzsche and Heidegger, as well as Zen. Translated by Jan Van Bragt in 1982, it is the most influential Kyoto School book in the West.

title: Mind and Nature (Xinti yu xingti)
creator: Mou Zongsan
description: In this massive study Mou Zongsan reads the Song and Ming Confucians as builders of a 'moral metaphysics' in which the moral mind is identical with the creative reality of the universe. He argues that the main line ran through Zhou Dunyi, Zhang Zai, Cheng Hao, Hu Hong, Liu Zongzhou, and Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming, while Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi, by separating principle from mind, made principle static and formed a 'side branch' that nonetheless became orthodoxy. The thesis has been much debated, but the work changed the study of Neo-Confucianism and is the centrepiece of Mou's philosophy.

title: Phenomenon and the Thing-in-Itself (Xianxiang yu wuzishen)
creator: Mou Zongsan
description: Kant held that human beings know only phenomena, because only an infinite mind could have intellectual intuition of things in themselves. In this book Mou Zongsan argues that Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist traditions all claim that the human mind can become infinite, through the moral mind, the Daoist mind of emptiness or the Buddhist mind of wisdom, and so can know things in themselves. He builds a 'two-level ontology' of an attached, phenomenal level and an unattached, noumenal one, and describes how the moral mind 'self-negates' to create the cognitive subject needed for science and democracy. It is the core of Mou's mature system and the most discussed work of contemporary New Confucian philosophy.
